description: Azure Table and Blob storage-aware state manager support for Egil.Orleans.Messaging.
releaseNotes:
BREAKING CHANGES:
- add a supported extension point for custom Event Hub batch containers
  `EnrichedEventHubAdapter` attaches its `EnrichedEventHubSequenceToken` by
  wrapping the base batch container in an internal decorator. An adapter that
  overrode `GetBatchContainer(EventHubMessage)` to decode its own payload format
  therefore lost the enrichment entirely, and the only workaround was to call
  `base.GetBatchContainer(...)` purely to read its `SequenceToken` and discard the
  rest — non-obvious, and it gave every event in the batch the batch-level token
  instead of a per-event index.
  Adapters now override `CreateInnerBatchContainer(EventHubMessage)` instead. The
  adapter keeps ownership of the wrapping, so the container only has to decode the
  payload; enqueue time, provider name, traceparent and per-event indexes are
  attached for it. A custom container does not need to produce sequence tokens at
  all — `null` batch and per-event tokens are supported, and per-event indexes then
  follow enumeration order.
  now sealed, so enrichment cannot be silently dropped. Adapters that overrode it
  move the body to `CreateInnerBatchContainer(EventHubMessage)` and drop the
  `base.GetBatchContainer(...)` call used to obtain a sequence token.
  Closes #185
- defer state writes on IStateManager<T>
  IStateManager<T> had one way to change what State returns: WriteAsync, which
  always goes to storage. State now has a setter, so a grain can move its visible
  snapshot forward and pay for the write later — the same shape as assigning
  IPersistentState<T>.State, which has never persisted on its own either.
      state.State = state.State with { Outbox = state.State.Outbox.RemoveRange(delivered) };
      await state.SaveChangesAsync(cancellationToken);
  HasUnsavedChanges reports a value that has been assigned and not written.
  SaveChangesAsync persists it, and does nothing when there is nothing
  outstanding.
  The motivating case is an outbox acknowledgement. In the consumer this library
  was extracted from, roughly one write in four to grain storages that own an
  outbox existed only to persist an acknowledgement. Deferring that removal is
  safe because items only leave the durable outbox once the removal is written,
  so losing one causes a redelivery and never a lost message.
  WriteAsync(newState) is unchanged, and keeps the guarantee that earns it a
  separate name: the value becomes visible only if the write succeeded. That is
  the difference between the two ways to persist.
      State = x then SaveChangesAsync()   visible immediately, durable at the save
      WriteAsync(x)                       visible only if it persisted
  The committed-state fence is narrowed precisely rather than quietly. A write
  candidate is a value whose durability is unknown because a write is running,
  and State still never exposes one. An unsaved value is one whose durability is
  knowingly deferred, and State does expose it — so an [AlwaysInterleave] reader
  can answer from a value that vanishes if the activation ends without persisting
  it.
  Persisting on the way out is the grain's job. A lifecycle observer never
  receives the DeactivationReason and the stop token is routinely already
  cancelled, so the library cannot do it. Call SaveChangesAsync unconditionally
  from OnDeactivateAsync: filtering on the reason means every code you skip is
  one that drops unsaved data. Live migration is one of those reasons — this
  library takes no part in Orleans' migration handoff, and Orleans runs
  OnDeactivateAsync before it dehydrates, so that write lands first and the
  destination inherits a durable value.
  Two smaller changes ride along.
  RegisterStateManager(storage) resolves an unkeyed IStateManagerFactory, so a
  grain naming its facet in [PersistentState] no longer repeats a name at the
  registration call. Register one with AddDefaultStateManager(). The named
  overloads still select provider-specific failure handling.
  Wrapping a journaled facet now throws. Orleans.Journaling's DurableState<T> is
  an IPersistentState<T>, and that package registers one for every DI key, so it
  can reach RegisterStateManager by accident. Its ReadStateAsync is a no-op, so
  this manager's read-back recovery would compare an attempted write with itself
  and report a failure as a success.
  HasUnsavedChanges and SaveChangesAsync(CancellationToken). This breaks custom
  implementations at source and at binary — an assembly compiled against an
  earlier version no longer satisfies the interface — so recompile consumers
  rather than mixing versions. Managers deriving from StateManagerBase<T> inherit
  the members and need no change. WriteAsync(T, CancellationToken) is unchanged.
  Wrapping an Orleans.Journaling facet, previously silently unsafe, now throws
  NotSupportedException at construction.
New Features:
- add single-type-argument AddStreamPostman for token enrichment
  Stamping a payload with something from its delivery token — the recommended
  alternative to storing the sender in the outbox message — returns the same type
  it receives, but the only token-aware projection overloads were
  AddStreamPostman<TSub, TEvent>. Neither type argument is inferable there, and
  C# has no partial type-argument inference, so the payload type had to be written
  twice.
  Enriching projections now name the payload type once, with either stream
  selector shape, on both direct registration and inside ForStreamProvider:
      .AddStreamPostman<SessionDataChangedEvent>(
          message => message.SessionId.GetSessionGrainStreamId(),
          (message, token) => message with { Source = token.Sender.ToString() })
  Existing registrations are unaffected: explicit type arguments and argument
  counts keep every previous call bound to the same overload. A call that omits
  type arguments entirely, using explicitly typed lambdas whose projection returns
  exactly the payload type, now reports an ambiguity instead of compiling; adding
  the single type argument resolves it.
- add Outbox<T>.Restore for rebuilding stored history
  Add and AddRange capture the current Activity so a delivered message links back
  to the request that produced it. That is right when a grain appends during a
  request, and wrong when an application rebuilds an outbox from previously
  persisted data: an IMigrateFrom implementation, an import, or a replay runs
  under whatever activity happens to be current — for a migration inside grain
  state deserialization, the activation — and that activity did not produce the
  messages. The delivery span then links orleans.outbox.post to an unrelated
  trace, which is worse than no link at all, because a wrong link is
  indistinguishable from a right one when reading a trace.
  Outbox<T>.Restore is the entry point for those paths, and never reads
  Activity.Current:
      Outbox<T>.Restore(messages)          payloads paired with their original timestamps
      Outbox<T>.Restore(messages, utcNow)  one timestamp, for formats that kept none per message
      Outbox<T>.Restore(envelopes)         full fidelity, preserving stored ids and traceparents
  The first two keep sequence assignment inside the outbox: consecutive numbers
  from 1, with the first timestamp as the epoch, and timestamps need not be
  ordered. The envelope overload is the one entry point that accepts
  caller-supplied identity, so it validates it — sequence numbers must strictly
  increase in enumeration order and all envelopes must share one epoch, because
  Remove only matches a FIFO head and receivers deduplicate against a per-epoch
  high-water mark. Traceparents on restored envelopes are carried through
  verbatim, including values that are not parseable W3C traceparents; delivery
  already tolerates those by starting an unlinked span, and rejecting them would
  fail a grain activation over a diagnostic field.
  Collection expressions still capture the ambient activity and cannot be given a
  suppressing form, so they remain the wrong tool for a rebuild — beyond the
  traceparent, they also reset the epoch and sequence space.
  Purely additive: Add, AddRange, and collection-expression construction are
  unchanged, and consumers need no recompile.
- make Event Hubs stream token converter registration public
  EventHubStreamSequenceTokenJsonConverters is now public, with Register() and the
  two type descriptors it uses as constants, and a companion
  services.AddEventHubStreamSequenceTokenJsonConverters() extension for callers
  with a container.
  Only UseEnrichedDataAdapter() could register these converters before, so a
  process that reads the same persisted grain state without configuring an Event
  Hub stream provider had to copy three descriptor strings and three converter
  constructions: a test fixture on in-memory storage using the production
  JsonSerializerOptions, a tool that reads grain state blobs offline, a background
  archiver. Without the converters, StreamCursor and MessageTracker throw on any
  persisted Event Hub token.
  Registration is idempotent, so the new entry points and UseEnrichedDataAdapter()
  compose in any order and a silo doing both is fine.
  Tests cover round-tripping every Event Hub token type through StreamCursor,
  repeated registration, registering before UseEnrichedDataAdapter(), and that
  UseEnrichedDataAdapter() registers the converters at all, which nothing asserted
  previously. The test project's own copy of the three registration lines is
  replaced by the public call.
  Closes #184
- add TryRegister to the stream sequence token converter registry
  StreamSequenceTokenJsonConverters.TryRegister reports the outcome of a
  registration instead of throwing, for callers that want to surface a conflicting
  converter rather than catch one. It returns true when the registry holds an
  equivalent converter once the call returns — whether it added one or found an
  identical one already present — and false when a different converter owns the
  type descriptor and was left in place.
  The return value answers "is my converter in place for this descriptor?", not
  "did this call mutate the registry", so a caller can treat false as a genuine
  conflict worth reporting.
  Register keeps its existing behaviour and now documents it: re-registering the
  same descriptor with the same token type and converter type is a no-op, and
  InvalidOperationException covers only a genuine conflict where a different
  converter claims a descriptor. Several registrars legitimately want the same
  converter in place, so their order carries no meaning.
